questions.statement:
A One-Man Recycling Revolution on The Cornish Coast
By Rupert Neate
01
Ian Falconer kept thinking ___ the heaps of discarded plastic fishing nets he saw at Newlyn
02 harbour near his home ___ Cornwall, England. Falconer, 52, who studied environmental and
03 mining geology ___ university, came up with a plan: shredding and cleaning the worn-out nets,
04 melting the plastic down, and converting it ___ filament to be used in 3D printing. He then built
05 a “micro-factory” so that the filament could be made into useful stuff. “Every year, up to 1 million
06 tonnes of fishing nets are discarded,” he says. “Most of that ends up in landfill or is burned, or
07 worse still, finds its way back into the oceans. This showed there was another way for some of
08 that material”.
09
The first big challenge he encountered when he started in 2016 was getting hold of the nets.
10 But he badgered the Newlyn harbour master into giving him a few to test his theory in his kitchen.
11 Since its launch the following year, Falconer’s company OrCA has raised more than £1m from
12 small investors in over 40 countries. The investment funded the development of patented new
13 machinery that can convert more than 20 kilos of nylon fishing nets an hour. He claims the
14 recycling process has less than 3% of the carbon impact of producing new nylon.
15
The nets that go into the shredder come out as small blue-green beads that Falconer sells
16 to 3D printing companies, which convert them into strings of filament used in 3D printing. They
17 also get sold around the world to replace new plastic in more conventional products that are
18 made using injection moulding. Falconer’s shipping container office is full of items made from
19 the raw material: sunglasses, light shades, bottle openers, razor blade handles. It can be used
20 for just about anything. The items he is most proud of are those made from his nylon mixed with
21 waste carbon fibre – mostly from offcuts of car and aeroplane manufacturi

Mark the INCORRECT statement about the highlighted word “profitable” (l. 34).

options.text: It is derived from the noun “profit”.
It means “making or likely to make a profit”.
It could be replaced by “enjoyable” with no significant changes in the meaning of the sentence.

questions.explanation: 'Profitable' é adjetivo derivado de 'profit' e significa lucrativo, capaz de gerar lucro. 'Enjoyable' significa agradável ou prazeroso, ideia distinta da rentabilidade; por isso a substituição altera o sentido do contexto.

questions.statement:
The secret history of Stonehenge
By James Owens
01
Stonehenge, located in southern England, ranks among the world’s most iconic
02 archaeological sites and one of its greatest enigmas. The megalithic stone circle on Salisbury
03 Plain inspires awe and fascination — but also intense debate some 4,600 years after it was built
04 by ancient Britons who left no written record.
05
The monument’s mysterious past has spawned countless tales and theories. According to
06 folklore, Stonehenge was created ___ Merlin, the wizard of Arthurian legend, who magically
07 transported the massive stones ___ Ireland, where giants had assembled them.
08
Another legend says invading Danes put the stones up, and another theory says they were
09 the ruins of a Roman temple. Modern-day interpretations are no less colorful. Some argue that
10 Stonehenge is a spacecraft landing area for aliens, and even more say it’s a giant fertility symbol
11 in the shape of female genitalia.
12
Archaeological investigation of the site dates back to the 1660s, when it was first surveyed
13 by antiquarian John Aubrey. He wrongly credited Stonehenge to the much later Celts, believing
14 it to be a religious center presided over by Druid priests.
15
Centuries of fieldwork since show the Neolithic monument, now a UNESCO World Heritage
16 site, was more than a millennium in the making. It started out 5,000 years ago as a circular
17 earthen bank and ditch, in a larger area of burial mounds.
18
Modern debate over the monument’s meaning has two main camps: those who see it as a
19 holy site, and others who believe it represents a scientific observatory.
20
Both camps base their theories on the site’s celestial influence. They point to alignments to
21 the sun and moon as evidence of rituals linked to the changing seasons and
22 the summer and winter solstices.
23
A radical theory asserts that Stonehenge served as a “prehistoric Lourdes” where people
24 came to be healed. This idea revolves around the smaller blue

What do the words in bold “who” (l. 04) and “he” (l. 29) refer to, respectively?
questions.explanation: O relativo 'who' retoma 'ancient Britons', os antigos britânicos que não deixaram registros escritos. Já 'he' retoma o pesquisador Mike Parker Pearson no contexto posterior do texto; os demais pares associam os pronomes a referentes incompatíveis.

In Portuguese, the underlined word “awe” (l. 03) means:
questions.explanation: Em 'inspires awe and fascination', 'awe' designa admiração profunda, reverência ou assombro diante de algo grandioso. O contexto de Stonehenge favorece esse sentido, não presunção, intimidade, otimismo ou intenção.

Which word is closest in meaning to “burial” in the sentence “in a larger area of burial mounds” (l. 17)?
questions.explanation: 'Burial' refere-se a sepultamento, por isso 'interment' é sinônimo adequado em 'burial mounds', isto é, montes funerários. 'Exhumation' e 'disinterment' designam retirada de restos mortais, e os demais termos não nomeiam sepultamento.
